blocks.text: The atmosphere has four distinct layers, defined by the change of temperature with increasing altitude (Figure 14.1).

items: Troposphere: the lowest region, extending up to 12 km. It includes all the major gases, nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and so on; the temperature decreases regularly from 17 degrees C to -58 degrees C. It is the densest layer, and the layer in which the major events such as rain, lightning and hurricanes occur.

Stratosphere: above the troposphere, 12 to 50 km above the earth's surface; the temperature increases from -58 degrees C to -2 degrees C. It can be divided into three regions according to the ultraviolet radiation that reaches them. Ozone in the upper layer absorbs high-energy ultraviolet radiation and breaks down into monatomic and diatomic oxygen, O3 gives O2 + O. The middle stratosphere has less ultraviolet passing through it, and here monatomic and diatomic oxygen recombine to form ozone in an exothermic reaction, O2 + O gives O3, which is how the ozone layer forms. The lower stratosphere receives very little ultraviolet, so monatomic oxygen is not found and ozone is not formed there.
Mesosphere: about 50 to 85 km from the ground; the temperature decreases with altitude from -2 degrees C to -93 degrees C, and the coldest region of the atmosphere lies in this layer.

Thermosphere: 85 km to 600 km above the surface; the temperature increases with altitude because energetic ultraviolet and X-rays are absorbed; in the upper thermosphere it can range from 500 degrees C to 2000 degrees C or higher.

blocks.long_description: Nitrogen and oxygen make up nearly all of the air, with argon and carbon dioxide as minor gases and a handful of trace gases. Going upward, temperature falls through the dense troposphere where weather happens, rises through the stratosphere because ozone there absorbs ultraviolet light, falls again through the mesosphere to the coldest point, and then rises steeply in the thermosphere where ultraviolet and X-rays are absorbed. In the upper stratosphere ultraviolet light splits ozone into oxygen molecules and atoms, and in the middle stratosphere atoms and molecules recombine exothermically to rebuild the ozone layer, while the lower stratosphere receives too little ultraviolet to make ozone at all.

blocks.prompt: Give the equations for the formation and depletion of ozone in the stratosphere, and explain the temperature trends of the troposphere and stratosphere (Quick Check 14.1b, c; exercise Q.2c).
blocks.explanation: Depletion in the upper stratosphere: O3 with ultraviolet gives O2 + O; formation in the middle stratosphere: O2 + O gives O3 (exothermic). The troposphere is heated from below by the warmed ground, so it cools with height; the stratosphere is heated from within because its ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and the recombination releases heat, so its temperature rises with height.

items: Four layers by temperature trend: troposphere 0-12 km (cools to -58 degrees C, weather, densest); stratosphere 12-50 km (warms to -2 degrees C; ozone: O3 gives O2 + O, O2 + O gives O3); mesosphere 50-85 km (coldest, -93 degrees C); thermosphere 85-600 km (500-2000 degrees C, absorbs UV and X-rays).
